items.passage: Photography is commonly regarded as an aid to memory, but psychologist Linda Henkel has found that it can impair recollection. Participants guided through an art museum were instructed to observe certain objects and to photograph others; when tested subsequently, they remembered fewer of the objects they had photographed in their entirety and recalled fewer of those objects’ details. When participants instead zoomed in to photograph a particular feature of an object, however, no such impairment emerged: their memory for features outside the frame was as strong as their memory for those within it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a study indicating that photographing objects can impair memory of them, an effect the researcher attributes to people’s reliance on cameras to remember for them.
It describes a study in which museum visitors who zoomed in to photograph part of an object later remembered more about it than visitors who simply looked.
It summarizes research suggesting that photographing objects can weaken people’s memory of them, though how the photographs are taken may make a difference.
It reports a finding that photographing objects impairs memory of them and that zooming in on one feature also weakens memory of the features left outside the frame.
items.explanation: The text reports that participants “remembered fewer of the objects they had photographed in their entirety and recalled fewer of those objects’ details,” and then turns: “When participants instead zoomed in to photograph a particular feature of an object, however, no such impairment emerged.” Choice C names both parts of the account: photographing can weaken memory, but the way the photograph is taken may change that result.

A.why_wrong: The text does say that photographing objects can impair memory, but it never offers an explanation for the effect, so nothing in it attributes the effect to people relying on their cameras. The option also leaves out the zoomed-in exception.

B.why_wrong: The text says only that when participants zoomed in, “no such impairment emerged”; it does not say they remembered more than participants who simply observed the objects.

D.recipe: first clause true, later clause reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The text agrees that photographing whole objects impaired memory, but it says that when participants zoomed in, “no such impairment emerged”: their memory for features outside the frame “was as strong as their memory for those within it.”

sources.what: Henkel (2014, Psychological Science): museum tour; photographing whole objects impaired memory for the objects and their details; zooming in on a part removed the impairment, and memory for parts outside the zoom was as strong as for those inside it

items.notes: Area: social science (psychology). Key C. Key parts: 2 (photographing can weaken memory; the manner of photographing may matter). Band-7 checks: key 23 words, hedged dual purpose; A and D keep a true first clause and fail later (invented cause; zooming said to weaken memory outside the frame), B overreaches the exception into a benefit. Option openings varied to avoid a shared prefix. 'When tested later' simplifies the next-day test.

band7.why: Hedged dual-purpose key paraphrased away from the passage; A and D are right in their first clause and fail only later (an invented cause; a reversed detail about features outside the frame), B stretches the exception into a benefit: the shape of 82cb7dda.

fixes: D rebuilt: was 'no matter which part of an object they focus on', a flat contradiction of the turn; now right in its first clause and wrong only on the detail about features outside the frame

band7.why: Hedged dual-purpose key paraphrased away from the passage; A and D are right in their first clause and fail only later (an invented cause; a reversed detail about features outside the frame), B stretches the exception into a benefit: the shape of 82cb7dda.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Selma Lagerlöf’s 1891 novel The Story of Gösta Berling (translated by Pauline Bancroft Flach in 1898). The major’s wife owns Ekeby, an estate where a group of gentlemen live as her guests.

A harsh and capable woman is she, the major’s wife at Ekeby. She sleeps like a waggoner on the stable floor, with a meal-bag under her head. She swears like a trooper, and rules over her seven estates like a king; rules her own parish and all the neighboring parishes; yes, the whole of lovely Värmland. But for the homeless gentlemen she had been like a mother, and therefore they had closed their ears when slander had whispered to them that she was in league with the devil.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It portrays a woman as strong and commanding and suggests that the gentlemen she shelters disregard the rumors about her because they fear her power.
It portrays a woman of great strength and authority while suggesting why the people who rely on her have refused to think ill of her.
It recounts how a woman who once worked as a waggoner rose to become the ruler of an entire province.
It describes a woman whose rough habits have exposed her to rumors, rumors that the text suggests even the gentlemen she shelters have come to believe.
items.explanation: Most of the text shows the major’s wife as a forceful figure who “rules over her seven estates like a king.” The last sentence turns to the gentlemen she shelters: “for the homeless gentlemen she had been like a mother, and therefore they had closed their ears when slander had whispered to them” about her. Choice B covers both parts: her strength and authority, and the reason those who depend on her refuse to believe ill of her.

A.recipe: first clause true, later link wrong (INV motive)
A.why_wrong: The text does present her as strong and commanding, and the gentlemen do ignore the rumors, but it gives a different reason: “for the homeless gentlemen she had been like a mother, and therefore they had closed their ears.” Nothing suggests they act out of fear.

C.why_wrong: “Like a waggoner” and “like a king” are comparisons describing how she lives and rules; the text gives no history of her working as a waggoner or rising to rule a province.

D.recipe: first part plausible, later part reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The text never ties the rumors to her habits, and it says the gentlemen “had closed their ears when slander had whispered to them,” that is, they refused to listen to the rumors rather than believing them.

sources.what: Lagerlöf, The Story of Gösta Berling, trans. Pauline Bancroft Flach (Boston: Little, Brown, 1898); excerpt copied exactly, two sentences cut (adapted); Swedish original 1891
first published 1891; Flach translation 1898; the major's wife in charge of Ekeby

items.notes: Literature (novel in translation, pre-1910 prose). Key B. Key parts: 2 (her strength and authority; why her dependents refuse to think ill of her). Band-7 checks: key 25 words, dual purpose; A keeps the true first half and the right behavior but gives the wrong motive (fear), D reverses the gentlemen's response to the rumors, C literalizes two similes (the literary LIT trap). Cut from the original paragraph: 'She can lift a barrel of flour on her broad shoulders.', 'She follows the loads of ore ...', 'In the winter she will watch ...', 'She is a powerful woman.'

band7.why: Pre-1910 prose with inverted syntax (the band-7 literary profile); abstract dual key ('refused to think ill of her' for 'closed their ears when slander had whispered'); A and D now keep a true first part and fail on the motive or on the gentlemen's response, C literalizes the similes.

fixes: A rebuilt: was 'stay at Ekeby chiefly because they are afraid of her', killed by 'like a mother'; now keeps the gentlemen ignoring the rumors and fails only on the motive
D rebuilt: was 'suspicions well founded', killed by 'slander'; now fails on 'closed their ears' (they refused to listen, not believed)
notes: translator's preface in the Gutenberg file dates the Swedish original to 1894; 1891 kept (Wikipedia and standard first-publication year)

band7.why: Pre-1910 prose with inverted syntax (the band-7 literary profile); abstract dual key ('refused to think ill of her' for 'closed their ears when slander had whispered'); A and D now keep a true first part and fail on the motive or on the gentlemen's response, C literalizes the similes.

items.passage: Until the mid-twentieth century, most scholars regarded Gullah, the language of Black communities on the Sea Islands of South Carolina and Georgia, as a substandard variety of English, a jumble of mispronunciations and grammatical errors. After extensive fieldwork in those communities, linguist Lorenzo Dow Turner concluded instead that Gullah had been strongly influenced by African languages. His 1949 book Africanisms in the Gullah Dialect documented <u>more than 300 words and almost 4,000 personal names derived from languages of Africa</u>, and its research was so meticulous that it persuaded some scholars who had previously dismissed Gullah to reconsider.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It indicates how much evidence Turner gathered, evidence that the text suggests convinced most scholars of his time that Gullah had little connection to English.
It indicates how much evidence Turner gathered, evidence that the text suggests came mainly from written records rather than from Gullah speakers.
It identifies the African languages that contributed the most words to Gullah, a question the text indicates earlier scholars had debated.
It indicates how much evidence Turner gathered, evidence that the text suggests helps account for the book’s effect on some scholars.
items.explanation: Turner concluded that Gullah “had been strongly influenced by African languages,” and the underlined portion gives the size of the evidence in his book: “more than 300 words and almost 4,000 personal names.” The sentence then says the research “was so meticulous that it persuaded some scholars who had previously dismissed Gullah to reconsider.” The figures show how much evidence Turner assembled, which helps explain that effect, as choice D says.

A.recipe: first clause true, later clause overreaches (BROAD)
A.why_wrong: The underlined portion does show how much evidence Turner gathered, and the book did change some minds, but the text says it persuaded “some scholars who had previously dismissed Gullah to reconsider,” not most scholars, and it says Gullah was “strongly influenced by African languages,” not that it had little connection to English.

B.recipe: first clause true, later clause contradicted (INV)
B.why_wrong: The figures do measure Turner’s evidence, but the text says he reached his conclusion “after extensive fieldwork in those communities,” so nothing suggests the evidence came mainly from written records.

C.why_wrong: The underlined portion gives counts of words and names; it does not name any African languages or rank their contributions, and the text mentions no debate about which languages contributed most.

sources.what: Gullah language (Wikipedia): before Turner, mainstream scholars viewed Gullah as substandard English; Turner's fieldwork; over 300 African loanwords and almost 4,000 African personal names; Africanisms in the Gullah Dialect (1949); some academics changed their minds because the book was so well researched

items.notes: Area: history and humanities (linguistics). Key D. Key parts: 2 (the span shows the scale of the evidence; that scale helps explain the book's effect stated later in the same sentence). Band 7: the span is a figure of extent (as in 2e744883, 'more than 7,000 in all'), a means rather than the main claim; the deciding clause follows the span. A, B and the key share the lead 'It indicates how much evidence Turner gathered, evidence that the text suggests' (the a2f64e58 pattern); A fails on 'most scholars' and 'little connection to English', B on written records rather than fieldwork. Key 21 words. 'Until the mid-twentieth century' simplifies 'before Turner's work'.

band7.why: Span is a figure of extent, not the claim (as in 2e744883); the deciding clause follows the span; A, B and the key share one lead and differ only in the later link (overreach, written records, effect on scholars).

fixes: key D given the same opening as A and B (A and B had shared a 12-word lead the key lacked, so a test-wise student could drop them as a pair)
A rebuilt: was 'judged to be weaker than his book claimed', killed by 'persuaded'; now partly right (it did change minds) and fails on 'most scholars' and 'little connection to English'
notes: Gullah appears in official items (basketry, museums) and a w2 Words in Context item (Daughters of the Dust); Turner's linguistics is a different subject

band7.why: Span is a figure of extent, not the claim (as in 2e744883); the deciding clause follows the span; A, B and the key share one lead and differ only in the later link (overreach, written records, effect on scholars).

items.passage: From the 1920s into the 1970s, Kiowa photographer Horace Poolaw documented life in and around Mountain View, Oklahoma, producing portraits of relatives, friends, and tribal leaders and photographing the Indian fairs he attended as both spectator and official photographer. His images differ markedly from those of non-Native photographers such as Edward Curtis, who often portrayed Native peoples as a “vanishing race.” Poolaw instead depicted Kiowa people as active participants in contemporary American life who also took pride in their Native heritage. Much of his work reached a wide audience only after his death, when his daughter Linda had it printed, catalogued, and exhibited.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe a photographer’s body of work and explain what distinguished it from other photographs of Native peoples made in his era
To explain how Poolaw’s photographs led non-Native photographers such as Edward Curtis to change the way they portrayed Native peoples
To describe how Poolaw’s daughter found and preserved a collection of photographs that her father had kept private throughout his life
To argue that Poolaw’s photographs of Indian fairs are more historically valuable than his portraits of family members and tribal leaders
items.explanation: The text first describes what Poolaw photographed over five decades, then says his images “differ markedly from those of non-Native photographers such as Edward Curtis,” since Poolaw “depicted Kiowa people as active participants in contemporary American life.” The last sentence adds how his work later reached a wide audience. Choice A states this purpose: to describe the work and explain what set it apart.

B.why_wrong: The text contrasts Poolaw’s images with Curtis’s but never says Poolaw influenced Curtis or any other photographer.

C.why_wrong: Only the last sentence concerns Poolaw’s daughter, and the text says she had his work printed, catalogued, and exhibited; it never says she found it or that he kept it private.

D.recipe: stance and ranking the text does not make (STANCE)
D.why_wrong: The text mentions both the fair photographs and the portraits but does not rank them or argue that either is more valuable.

sources.what: Horace Poolaw (Wikipedia): Kiowa photographer from Mountain View, Oklahoma; work from the 1920s to the 1970s; portraits of family, friends and Kiowa leaders; Indian fairs as spectator and official photographer; differs from non-Native photographers such as Edward Curtis, who portrayed a 'vanishing race'; showed Native Americans as part of contemporary America and proud of their culture; daughter Linda had the work printed, catalogued and exhibited after his death in 1984

items.notes: Area: humanities (photography). Key A. band_target 6: P_profile has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/text_structure_and_purpose.md, assignment table), so written as a strong band 6 with a two-part key like 3.18 ('describe ... and explain how ...'). Distractors: B invents an influence on Curtis, C turns the last sentence into the purpose and adds a false detail, D adds a ranking.

band7.why: P_profile has no band-7 official items (band7 assignment table), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 like 3.18, two-part key, distractors INV, PART plus invented detail, STANCE.
P_profile has no band-7 official items (band7 assignment table), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 like 3.18, two-part key, distractors INV, PART plus invented detail, STANCE.

items.passage: Many students now take class notes on laptops, a habit that a widely cited 2014 study appeared to discourage: participants who wrote their notes by hand outperformed those who typed them on later tests of lecture content. But conclusions about the superiority of handwritten notes may be premature: when psychologist Kayla Morehead and colleagues repeated the 2014 experiment, some trends favored longhand, yet test performance did not consistently differ between groups—not even between students who took notes and students who took none. Pooling the results of several such repetitions, the team found only a small, statistically unreliable advantage for writing by hand.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that students should take notes on laptops because typing allows them to record more of what is said during a lecture
To describe a study showing that students who take no notes at all perform as well on tests as students who take notes by any method
To explain why participants in the 2014 study who typed their notes performed worse on tests than those who wrote by hand
To present research suggesting that a reported advantage of one way of taking notes is less certain than an earlier study implied
items.explanation: The text begins with a 2014 study in which students who wrote notes by hand “outperformed those who typed them,” then cautions that “conclusions about the superiority of handwritten notes may be premature.” It supports that caution with a repetition of the study in which performance “did not consistently differ between groups” and pooled results showing only “a small, statistically unreliable advantage.” Choice D states this purpose.

A.recipe: stance the text does not take (STANCE)
A.why_wrong: The text questions how strong the case for handwriting is, but it never recommends laptops or says typing records more of a lecture.

B.why_wrong: The text says performance did not consistently differ, even from a no-notes group, in one repetition; it does not present a study showing that taking notes is of no use, and that detail supports the larger caution about handwriting rather than being the text’s purpose.

C.why_wrong: The text reports the 2014 result but offers no explanation of why typists did worse; its focus is on whether the result holds up.

sources.what: Morehead, Dunlosky and Rawson (2019, Educational Psychology Review): direct replication of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014), which concluded longhand is superior; some trends favored longhand but performance did not consistently differ between groups, including a no-notes group; meta-analysis of direct replications showed small nonsignificant effects favoring longhand; concluding which method is superior seems premature

items.notes: Area: social science (educational psychology). Key D. band_target 6 (planned). Modeled on c61a7c4a (a caution stated, then a study as the case in point). Key hedged ('suggesting', 'less certain') to match the source's 'seems premature'. B is the near miss: it overstates one detail (no-notes group) into a finding about note-taking in general. The eWriter group of the replication is left out.

band7.why: Planned and written as band 6 (P_view has band-7 official c61a7c4a, but the plan cell is 6); hedged abstract key, B a near miss that overstates one detail into the purpose.
Planned and written as band 6 (P_view has band-7 official c61a7c4a, but the plan cell is 6); hedged abstract key, B a near miss that overstates one detail into the purpose.

items.passage: Chemist Ruth Benerito spent most of her career at the US Department of Agriculture’s Southern Regional Research Center in New Orleans, Louisiana, where she accumulated 55 patents. Beginning in the 1950s, she helped develop a technique for treating cotton through cross-linking, in which chemical bonds formed between adjacent cellulose molecules prevent the fibers from shifting, so that the fabric resists wrinkling during laundering and wear; related treatments rendered cotton resistant to stains and flames. Wrinkle-resistant cotton has since been credited with rescuing the cotton industry.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a chemist’s career, details one of her contributions to textile research, and then reports her objection to the credit she received for it.
It introduces a scientist, explains how a process she helped develop works, and then indicates why that process has been considered important.
It profiles a researcher’s career, outlines the chemistry of one of her innovations, and then explains why that innovation was slow to catch on.
It describes a problem facing cotton growers, outlines several attempts to solve it, and then credits one chemist with the most successful solution.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Benerito and where she worked. The second explains the cross-linking technique she “helped develop,” in which chemical bonds “prevent the fibers from shifting, so that the fabric resists wrinkling.” The last sentence gives the work’s significance: wrinkle-resistant cotton “has since been credited with rescuing the cotton industry.” Choice B follows these three moves in order.

A.recipe: first two moves right, invented third move (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text does present Benerito’s career and one of her contributions, but it never reports any objection she made to the credit she received; its last sentence states why the work is considered important.

C.recipe: first two moves right, third move reversed (REV)
C.why_wrong: The text does profile Benerito and explain the chemistry of cross-linking, but it never says the treatment was slow to catch on; its last sentence says wrinkle-resistant cotton “has since been credited with rescuing the cotton industry.”

D.why_wrong: The text does not open with a problem facing cotton growers or describe several attempts to solve one; it opens by introducing Benerito.

sources.what: Ruth R. Benerito (Wikipedia): worked at USDA laboratories in New Orleans from the 1950s, mostly at the Southern Regional Research Center; process using cross-linking led to wrinkle-resistant (and stain- and flame-resistant) cotton; 55 patents; described as having saved the cotton industry; she said no one person was responsible ('I contributed to a new process')

items.notes: Area: natural science and history (chemistry). Key B. band_target 6: S13 has no band-7 official items (assignment table), so written as a strong band 6. 'Helped develop' and 'credited with' follow the source; she disclaimed sole credit, which A turns into an invented third move (the passage does not report it). Distractor shapes follow 3.6: one keeps moves 1 and 2 and breaks move 3 (A), one keeps moves 1 and 2 and reverses move 3 (C, added in review), one is a different template (D).

band7.why: S13 has no band-7 official items (its only model, 3.6, is band 4), so it cannot be band 7; hardened to a strong band 6: A and C keep moves 1 and 2 and break move 3.

fixes: C rebuilt: was a wholly wrong detail hook (laboratory, patents, clothing styles); now keeps moves 1 and 2 and reverses move 3

band7.why: S13 has no band-7 official items (its only model, 3.6, is band 4), so it cannot be band 7; hardened to a strong band 6: A and C keep moves 1 and 2 and break move 3.

items.passage: Even on days without major earthquakes, seismometers detect Earth vibrating continuously at characteristic low frequencies, a phenomenon called the “hum.” The hum’s daily energy is equivalent to that of an earthquake of roughly magnitude 6, far exceeding what the numerous small earthquakes occurring each day could collectively supply. Slow, or “silent,” earthquakes have likewise been ruled out as its source in all but a few instances. Instead, a team of seismologists is likely correct that the hum originates as storm energy is converted into long ocean waves interacting with the seafloor: the team traced it primarily to the northern Pacific and the southern oceans, each during its own hemisphere’s winter.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a natural process, rejects two explanations for it, and then concludes that no explanation proposed so far is convincing.
It presents a scientific observation, considers two proposed causes that the author finds unconvincing, and then cites seasonal evidence that supports one of them.
It introduces a geophysical phenomenon, indicates that two possible sources cannot account for it, and then offers an explanation the author considers probable.
It reports a geophysical discovery, explains how scientists first detected it, and then describes a debate about whether it poses any danger.
items.explanation: The text introduces the “hum,” Earth’s continuous vibration. It then rules out two sources: “the numerous small earthquakes occurring each day” could not supply enough energy, and slow earthquakes “have likewise been ruled out.” Finally it presents a third account, that the hum arises from storm energy in the oceans, which the author says a team “is likely correct” about. Choice C follows these moves and the author’s stance.

A.recipe: first two moves right, third move reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: The text does reject two explanations, but it then endorses a third, saying the team “is likely correct,” rather than concluding that no explanation is convincing.

B.recipe: first two moves right, third move misattached (INV)
B.why_wrong: The seasonal evidence supports the ocean-storm account, a third explanation; it does not support either of the two causes the text has already ruled out.

D.why_wrong: The text does not explain how the hum was first detected or describe any debate about danger; it weighs possible sources of the hum.

sources.what: Rhie and Romanowicz (2004, Nature): Earth's hum on days without significant earthquakes; daily excitation equivalent to magnitude 5.75 to 6.0 earthquakes, not explained by summing small earthquakes; slow or silent earthquakes ruled out except in a few isolated cases; sources mainly in the northern Pacific in northern winter and the southern oceans in southern winter; generated by atmosphere-ocean-seafloor coupling, probably storm energy converted to infragravity waves interacting with seafloor topography

items.notes: Area: natural science (seismology). Key C. Key parts: 3. Modeled on 6ae393f7 (3.11): phenomenon, two sources refuted, a third the author endorses ('is likely correct', matching the source's 'probably'). Researchers left unnamed: Barbara Romanowicz is named in an official Transitions item. Band-7 checks: A and B keep moves 1 and 2 and break move 3 (reversal; evidence misattached), D a different template. Option wording kept away from the official distractors.

band7.why: Matches 6ae393f7 move for move: phenomenon, two sources refuted, third endorsed with a hedge; A and B keep moves 1 and 2 and break move 3 (reversed stance; evidence misattached to a rejected cause).

fixes: B reworded: it shared an 8-word run with official 6ae393f7 B ('that the author regards as flawed, and then describes')

key C: 'explains why two possible sources cannot account for it' to 'indicates that ...' (the text gives no reason for ruling out slow earthquakes), and 'considers likely to be correct' to 'considers probable' (echoed the passage)
notes: Romanowicz is named in official Transitions 47e238be (Iceland magma), a different subject; researchers left unnamed here

band7.why: Matches 6ae393f7 move for move: phenomenon, two sources refuted, third endorsed with a hedge; A and B keep moves 1 and 2 and break move 3 (reversed stance; evidence misattached to a rejected cause).

items.passage:
The following text is from Henry Lawson’s 1896 short story collection While the Billy Boils. The narrator describes Golden Gully, an abandoned gold-mining area in Australia.

The predominant note of the scene was a painful sense of listening, that never seemed to lose its tension—a listening as though for the sounds of digger [gold miner] life, sounds that had gone and left a void that was accentuated by the signs of a former presence. The main army of diggers had long ago vanished to new rushes, leaving only its stragglers and deserters behind. These were men who were too poor to drag families about, men who were old and feeble, and men who had lost their faith in fortune.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To convey the emptiness of a once-busy mining area and describe the miners who have stayed
To describe a battle in which an army of miners was defeated and scattered across the countryside
To show that the miners who remain in Golden Gully are content with the quiet of the deserted field
To explain why the miners who left Golden Gully later regretted their decision to search elsewhere
items.explanation: The first sentence describes the scene as “a painful sense of listening” for “sounds that had gone and left a void,” which conveys how empty the place has become. The rest of the text says most miners “had long ago vanished” and describes those left behind: men “too poor,” “old and feeble,” or who “had lost their faith in fortune.” Choice A covers both parts.

B.why_wrong: “Army,” “stragglers,” and “deserters” describe the miners figuratively; the miners left for “new rushes,” and no battle takes place.

C.why_wrong: The text calls the scene’s silence “painful” and describes the remaining men as poor, feeble, or without faith in fortune, not content.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that the main body of miners “vanished to new rushes”; it says nothing about whether they regretted leaving.

sources.what: Henry Lawson, While the Billy Boils (1896), story “His Father’s Mate”; paragraph copied exactly up to 'faith in fortune', its last sentence left out, gloss added
While the Billy Boils published 1896

items.notes: Literature (short story collection, 1896). Key A, two-part like 2.6's 'the town and the people'. Distractors: B literalizes the army metaphor, C reverses the feeling, D invents a reaction. The source line names the 1896 collection because the excerpt is taken from that text (the story first appeared in 1888). Original '--' rendered as a closed em dash.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from William Makepeace Thackeray’s 1853–55 novel The Newcomes. Sir Barnes Newcome, a wealthy banker, owns an estate near the English town of Newcome.

In spite of all his subscriptions [donations], and his coaxing of the various orders of Newcomites, Sir Barnes Newcome was not popular among them; and while he had enemies on all sides, had sturdy friends not even on his own. People felt as if it was a truce only, and not an alliance with him, and always speculated on the possibility of war: when he turned his back on them in the market, men felt relieved, and, as they passed his gate, looked with no friendly glances over his park-wall.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe a long conflict between a man and his neighbors that ended in a formal truce
To show how a man’s generosity gradually won over the people of a town who had once distrusted him
To explain why a man refused to give money to the various groups in a town
To convey that a man’s efforts to win the goodwill of his neighbors have not earned their trust
items.explanation: The text says that “in spite of all his subscriptions [donations], and his coaxing” of the townspeople, Sir Barnes “was not popular among them.” It adds that people felt “it was a truce only, and not an alliance with him” and were “relieved” when he turned his back. Choice D states this purpose: his efforts to please the town have not won its trust.

A.why_wrong: “Truce,” “alliance,” and “war” describe how the townspeople feel about Sir Barnes; no actual conflict or formal truce is described.

B.why_wrong: The text says that despite his donations Sir Barnes “was not popular” and that people stayed wary of him, not that they were won over.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions “all his subscriptions [donations],” so it does not describe him refusing to give money.

sources.what: Thackeray, The Newcomes (Gutenberg text): paragraph adapted: the opening 'So,' and the middle sentence 'Scarce a man but felt Barnes was laughing at him; ... recovered their good-humour when he left them.' cut, otherwise copied exactly; Sir Barnes's banking house and estate from the novel
The Newcomes published in 24 monthly parts, October 1853 to August 1855

items.notes: Literature (novel). Key D. The text's war imagery (truce, alliance, war) supplies the LIT trap (A); B reverses the outcome; C contradicts the donations. Gloss [donations] added for 'subscriptions'.

fixes: source note: records the cut middle sentence ('Scarce a man but felt ...'), not only the opening 'So,'

items.passage: Panther chameleons (Furcifer pardalis) can change color within minutes during courtship or contests between males. Such changes have generally been attributed to the movement of pigment-containing structures within skin cells. But a team led by physicist Jérémie Teyssier and biologist Michel Milinkovitch found that the lizards <u>shift their color by actively adjusting the spacing of a lattice of tiny guanine crystals in a layer of skin cells called iridophores</u>, which changes the wavelengths of light the skin reflects. A deeper layer of iridophores containing larger crystals reflects much of the near-infrared light in sunlight, potentially helping keep the animals cool.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the movement of pigments that researchers had long thought was responsible for the lizards’ color changes.
It explains how the lizards accomplish the color changes mentioned at the beginning of the text.
It explains how the lizards’ skin protects them from overheating in direct sunlight.
It identifies the reason that male chameleons change color more often than female chameleons do.
items.explanation: The first sentence says panther chameleons “can change color within minutes.” The underlined portion explains how they do it: they “shift their color by actively adjusting the spacing of a lattice of tiny guanine crystals.” Choice B states this function.

A.why_wrong: The pigment explanation appears in the second sentence as the earlier view; the underlined portion presents the team’s different finding.

C.why_wrong: Protection from heat is the job of the last sentence, which describes a deeper layer of iridophores; the underlined portion concerns color change.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares how often males and females change color; it mentions contests between males only as one occasion for color change.

sources.what: Teyssier, Saenko, van der Marel and Milinkovitch (2015, Nature Communications): panther chameleons' rapid color change during male contests or courtship; generally interpreted as pigment dispersion/aggregation; actually active tuning of a lattice of guanine nanocrystals in superficial iridophores; a deeper iridophore layer with larger crystals reflects much sunlight, especially near-infrared, potentially giving thermal protection

items.notes: Area: natural science (biology and physics). Key B. The underlined span is a mechanism (as in 2.14 and 2.15). A uses the view the span overturns, C the following sentence's job, D an invented comparison. Teyssier is at Geneva's Department of Quantum Matter Physics; Milinkovitch at its Department of Genetics and Evolution.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Amy Levy’s 1889 poem “Cambridge in the Long.” The speaker, who has left a busy city, is spending the summer vacation in Cambridge, an English university town.

Where drowsy sound of college-chimes
Across the air is blown,
And drowsy fragrance of the limes [linden trees],
I lie and dream alone.

This is the place; it is not strange,
But known of old and dear.—
What went I forth to seek? The change
Is mine; why am I here?

Alas, in vain I turned away,
I fled the town in vain;
The strenuous life of yesterday
Calleth me back again.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker describes a peaceful refuge and then acknowledges that it has not released the speaker from a busier life.
The speaker recalls a familiar town and then explains how the town has changed since the speaker last saw it.
The speaker describes the noise and hurry of a city and then expresses relief at having finally escaped to a calmer place.
The speaker praises the beauty of a university and then urges others to visit it during the summer.
items.explanation: The first stanza pictures a quiet scene of “drowsy” chimes and fragrance where the speaker can “lie and dream alone.” The last stanza admits, “in vain I turned away, / I fled the town in vain,” since “the strenuous life of yesterday / Calleth me back again.” Choice A describes this movement from a peaceful retreat to the admission that the retreat has not freed the speaker.

B.recipe: word hook on “The change / Is mine” (LIT)
B.why_wrong: The speaker says “The change / Is mine,” meaning that the speaker has changed; the place is “known of old and dear” and “not strange,” so the poem does not describe the town changing.

C.why_wrong: The poem begins with the calm scene, not the city, and ends by saying the escape was “in vain,” not with relief.

D.why_wrong: The speaker never addresses or urges other people; the poem is about the speaker’s own failed retreat.

sources.what: Amy Levy, A London Plane-Tree, and Other Verse (1889), poem “Cambridge in the Long”; stanzas 1, 3 and 4 copied exactly (stanza 2 left out, so 'adapted'), gloss added
A London Plane-Tree and Other Verse (1889); Levy studied at Newnham College, Cambridge

items.notes: Literature (poem, 1889). Key A. Like 2.8, the speaker's effort (fleeing the town) meets a limit (the old life calls the speaker back). The context line tells the student the speaker came from a busy city, as CB context lines set up the situation. B is the medium trap: it reads 'The change / Is mine' as a change in the town.

notes: length 105 against a 63-word model poem; inside CB's medium literary range (max 146), kept

items.passage: Medieval bestiaries, such as the Aberdeen Bestiary and the Ashmole Bestiary, both produced in England around 1200, describe real and imaginary creatures indiscriminately and pair each animal with a Christian moral lesson, relying largely on earlier texts rather than on direct observation. But not every medieval treatment of animals depended on inherited authority. In the 1240s, Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II composed De arte venandi cum avibus (The Art of Hunting with Birds), a treatise that undertakes to describe birds as they actually are, reports experiments such as covering vultures’ eyes to determine whether they hunt by smell, and frequently contradicts Aristotle.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It compares two English manuscripts and then traces how their illustrations influenced a later book about falconry.
It describes two medieval books about animals and then argues that the moral lessons in such books rested on careful observation of nature.
It summarizes the history of falconry in medieval Europe and then describes a ruler’s efforts to protect certain birds.
It characterizes a kind of medieval book through two examples and then describes a work from the same period with a different approach.
items.explanation: The first sentence characterizes medieval bestiaries, naming “the Aberdeen Bestiary and the Ashmole Bestiary,” as books “relying largely on earlier texts rather than on direct observation.” The text then says “not every medieval treatment of animals depended on inherited authority” and describes Frederick II’s treatise, which “undertakes to describe birds as they actually are.” Choice D follows this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text does not compare the two bestiaries with each other or mention their illustrations or any influence on Frederick II’s book.

B.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)
B.why_wrong: The text does describe two bestiaries, but it says they relied on earlier texts “rather than on direct observation”; observation is what sets Frederick II’s book apart.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no history of falconry, and Frederick II’s treatise is described as a study of birds, not an effort to protect them.

sources.what: De arte venandi cum avibus (Wikipedia): written in the 1240s by Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II; aims to describe things as they are; experiments such as covering vultures' eyes to test whether they use smell while hunting; likes to contradict Aristotle

Bestiary (Wikipedia): each beast paired with a moral lesson; compilations of earlier texts; no distinction between existing and imaginary animals; Aberdeen Bestiary (12th century) and Ashmole Bestiary (early 13th century, England)

items.notes: Area: humanities and history (medieval books). Key D. Like 2.11: a field characterized through two named works, then a way some works in it differ. 'Around 1200' covers the Aberdeen (c. 1200) and Ashmole (early 13th century) bestiaries. Distractors: A wholly wrong, B keeps move 1 and reverses move 2, C a word hook (falconry).

items.passage: Because Islamic teachings prohibit drinking wine, one might expect that the Mediterranean wine trade, which had flourished under the Roman Empire, diminished in regions that subsequently came under Muslim rule. Recent chemical evidence complicates that expectation: analyzing residues preserved in more than 100 transport jars, or amphorae, dating from the fifth to the eleventh centuries, archaeologist Léa Drieu and colleagues determined that wine continued to be traded through Sicily while the island was under Islamic rule, with some exported from Palermo to ports under Christian control.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes how archaeologists identify the contents of ancient jars and then explains why that method has proved unreliable.
It presents an assumption that might seem reasonable and then describes recent findings that call it into question.
It presents two conflicting accounts of Sicily’s history and then describes a discovery that confirmed one of them.
It describes an expectation about trade under Muslim rule and then presents evidence that wine production ended in Sicily but continued elsewhere.
items.explanation: The first sentence sets out what “one might expect”: that the wine trade “diminished in regions that subsequently came under Muslim rule.” The text then says “recent chemical evidence complicates that expectation” and reports that wine “continued to be traded through Sicily while the island was under Islamic rule.” Choice B describes this structure.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template: method, then its flaw (INV)
A.why_wrong: The analysis of residues is mentioned only as how the team reached its finding; the text never says the method is unreliable.

C.recipe: wholly wrong template: conflicting accounts resolved (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text presents one expectation, not two conflicting accounts, and the finding complicates that expectation rather than confirming it.

D.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The text does open with an expectation about trade under Muslim rule, but the evidence shows that wine kept moving through Sicily, not that it stopped there.

sources.what: Drieu et al. (2021, PNAS): wine one of the most important Mediterranean commodities under the Roman Empire; less known whether trade continued under Islamic control; chemical analysis of 109 transport amphorae from the 5th to 11th centuries; wine continued to be traded through Sicily in the Islamic period, supplied locally and exported from Palermo to ports under Christian control; trade included products prohibited by the hadiths

items.notes: Area: history (archaeology). Key B. The source does not say scholars assumed the trade stopped, so move 1 is framed as what 'one might expect' and the key calls it 'an assumption that might seem reasonable'. Distractors: A and C are the official wholly-wrong templates in new words, D keeps move 1 and reverses move 2.

fixes: joined sentences 2 and 3 with a colon (batch medium words per sentence had dropped below check_rw's floor after item 11 was removed)

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Anthony Trollope’s 1861 novel Framley Parsonage. Mark Robarts, the son of a physician, has been educated alongside his close friend, the young Lord Lufton.

And then the lads went together to Oxford, and here Mark’s good fortune followed him, consisting rather in the highly respectable manner in which he lived, than in any wonderful career of collegiate success. His family was proud of him, and the doctor [Mark’s father] was always ready to talk of him to his patients; not because he was a prizeman, and had gotten medals and scholarships, but on account of the excellence of his general conduct. He lived with the best set—he incurred no debts—he was fond of society, but able to avoid low society—liked his glass of wine, but was never known to be drunk.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a young man’s academic honors and then explains why his family feared those honors would make him arrogant.
It presents a young man’s popularity at a university and then shows how that popularity drew him into debt.
It presents the high regard in which a young man is held and then describes the conduct on which that regard rests.
It contrasts a father’s hopes for his son with the son’s disappointing behavior at a university.
items.explanation: The text first says Mark’s “family was proud of him” and his father “was always ready to talk of him to his patients,” praising “the excellence of his general conduct.” It then lists that conduct: “he incurred no debts,” he could “avoid low society,” and he “was never known to be drunk.” Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text says Mark was praised “not because he was a prizeman, and had gotten medals and scholarships,” and it mentions no fear that he would become arrogant.

B.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)
B.why_wrong: The text says Mark “was fond of society” and “lived with the best set,” but it says plainly that “he incurred no debts.”

D.why_wrong: Mark’s conduct is described as excellent, and his father is proud of him; nothing in it disappoints.

sources.what: Trollope, Framley Parsonage (Gutenberg text), chapter 1: paragraph copied exactly up to 'never known to be drunk' (its last clause, 'and, above all things, was one of the most popular men in the university', cut, so 'adapted'); Mark's father is a physician at Exeter; Mark is educated with the young Lord Lufton
serialized in the Cornhill January 1860 to April 1861, book form April 1861; Mark Robarts the hero, a childhood friend of Lord Lufton

items.notes: Literature (novel). Key C. Same moves as 2.22 (the regard others hold, then the behaviors that sustain it) with a different tone: Trollope's regard is earned, Eliot's is managed. Distractors: A reverses the prizes detail, B keeps move 1 and reverses the debts detail, D reverses the evaluation. Gloss [Mark's father] added for 'the doctor'.

fixes: B why_wrong: no longer says the text notes Mark's popularity (that clause was cut from the excerpt); cites 'fond of society' and 'lived with the best set'
notes: length 137 (writer's 136 plus underline) against model 2.22 at 129 and CB's medium literary max of 146: kept; nothing can be cut without losing the regard or the conduct list

items.passage: Old collections of birds’ eggs are sometimes dismissed as relics of an outdated hobby, but they deserve better. In 1968, ecologists Joseph Hickey and Daniel Anderson compared peregrine falcon eggs in museum collections with eggs gathered in the 1960s and found the recent shells thinner, evidence that helped link the falcon’s decline to pesticides such as DDT. The original collectors could never have foreseen such a use, which is precisely why these collections should be preserved.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that old egg collections are valuable because they can answer questions no collector anticipated
To explain how the once-popular hobby of collecting birds’ eggs contributed to the decline of the peregrine falcon
To describe the methods that museums use to protect fragile eggshells from damage
To compare the eggs of peregrine falcons with the eggs of birds that were never exposed to DDT
items.explanation: The text says old egg collections “deserve better” than to be dismissed, gives the example of a study that used museum eggs to help “link the falcon’s decline to pesticides such as DDT,” and ends that the collectors “could never have foreseen such a use, which is precisely why these collections should be preserved.” Choice A states this argument.

B.why_wrong: The text links the falcon’s decline to pesticides, not to egg collecting.

C.why_wrong: The text never discusses how museums protect eggshells.

D.why_wrong: The text compares older and more recent peregrine eggs, not peregrine eggs with those of birds never exposed to DDT.

sources.what: Field Museum blog, 'Eggshells, DDT, Collections, and Study Design': Hickey and Anderson used museum collections, including the Field Museum's, to show that peregrine eggs from the 1960s were thinner; the original collectors had no idea their eggs would be used this way

items.notes: Area: natural science and humanities (museum collections). Key A. The argument is the author's own, with the evaluative markers CB keys 'argue' on ('deserve better', 'should be preserved'), as in 2.18. Hickey and Anderson's 1968 Science paper linked the thinning to chlorinated hydrocarbon pesticides; 'pesticides such as DDT' keeps to that. Distractors are INV, as in medium P_argue.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from George Washington Cable’s 1879 short story collection Old Creole Days. Colonel De Charleu owns Belles Demoiselles, a plantation on the Mississippi River in Louisiana.

How high that river was! Its tremendous current rolled and tumbled and spun along, hustling the long funeral flotillas of drift—and how near shore it came! Men were out day and night, watching the levee [embankment that holds back the river]. On windy nights even the old Colonel took part, and grew light-hearted with occupation and excitement, as <u>every minute the river threw a white arm over the levee’s top, as though it would vault over</u>. But all held fast, and, as the summer drifted in, the water sunk down into its banks and looked quite incapable of harm.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes a worker reaching over the levee to pull debris out of the river.
It conveys the Colonel’s fear that the levee would give way during the night.
It explains why the water eventually returned to its banks as summer arrived.
It emphasizes how close the rising river came to overflowing the levee.
items.explanation: The text describes a river so high that “men were out day and night, watching the levee.” The underlined image of the river throwing “a white arm over the levee’s top, as though it would vault over” shows the water repeatedly reaching the top of the levee, which emphasizes how near it came to spilling over, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The “white arm” is the river’s foaming water, described as if it were a limb; no worker reaches over the levee.

B.why_wrong: The text says the Colonel “grew light-hearted with occupation and excitement,” not fearful.

C.why_wrong: The water’s retreat is described in the last sentence; the underlined portion describes the river at its most threatening.

sources.what: Cable, Old Creole Days (Gutenberg text), story “Belles Demoiselles Plantation”; paragraph copied exactly except ',--' rendered as a closed em dash; gloss added; the master is old Colonel De Charleu
Old Creole Days published as a book in 1879

items.notes: Literature (short stories, 1879). Key D. Like 2.23, an image whose job is to show extent (here, of the flood's threat). B is the near miss: a student who assumes danger means fear misses 'light-hearted'. A literalizes the arm, C is the next sentence's job.

items.passage:
The following text is from Alice Brown’s 1899 short story collection Tiverton Tales. After her mother’s death, Lucy Ann has been staying with her brother’s family. She has now returned to the house where she lived with her mother.

<u>The first day in the old house seemed to her like new birth in Paradise.</u> She wandered about, touching chairs and tables and curtains, the manifest symbols of an undying past. There were loving duties to be done, but she could not do them yet. She had to look her pleasure in the face, and learn its lineaments.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that Lucy Ann finds the house unfamiliar after her long absence.
It emphasizes how happy Lucy Ann is to be back in her own home.
It describes the religious beliefs that comfort Lucy Ann after her mother’s death.
It explains what Lucy Ann must finish before her brother’s family visits her.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence compares Lucy Ann’s first day back to “new birth in Paradise,” an image of great joy. The rest of the text supports that reading: she wanders about “touching chairs and tables and curtains” and has to “look her pleasure in the face.” The sentence emphasizes her happiness at being home, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The house is full of “the manifest symbols of an undying past” that she lovingly touches; nothing suggests it feels unfamiliar to her.

C.why_wrong: “Paradise” is part of a comparison that expresses her joy; the text does not describe her religious beliefs.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions “loving duties” she cannot do yet, but the underlined sentence does not concern them, and no visit from her brother’s family is mentioned.

sources.what: Alice Brown, Tiverton Tales (1899), story “The Way of Peace”: Lucy Ann Cummings, after her mother's funeral, visits her brother John's family and then returns home; paragraph copied exactly

items.notes: Literature (short story collection, 1899). Key B. Like 1.1 ('emphasizes Shakti's sense of belonging in the landscape'), a simile whose job is to show a feeling. A reverses it, C literalizes 'Paradise', D is invented. Replaced a Higginson excerpt whose quoted wording shared generic 6-word runs with two live items.

items.passage:
The following text is from Elizabeth Gaskell’s 1858 novella My Lady Ludlow. The narrator and her friend Mary Mason, two young women who live in the household of Lady Ludlow, are meeting Mr. Gray, a clergyman who is new to the area.

He blushed redder than ever at the sight of us, as we entered the hall and dropped him our curtsies. <u>He coughed two or three times, as if he would have liked to speak to us, if he could but have found something to say; and every time he coughed he became hotter-looking than ever.</u> I am ashamed to say, we were nearly laughing at him; half because we, too, were so shy that we understood what his awkwardness meant.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that Mr. Gray has become ill with a fever.
It indicates that the narrator considers Mr. Gray rude.
It shows how embarrassed Mr. Gray feels in front of the narrator and Mary.
It explains why Mr. Gray has come to visit Lady Ludlow.
items.explanation: Mr. Gray “blushed redder than ever” when the young women came in. The underlined sentence adds that he coughed “as if he would have liked to speak to us, if he could but have found something to say,” and that he “became hotter-looking than ever.” These details show his embarrassment, which the narrator calls “his awkwardness,” as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: Mr. Gray looks “hotter” because he is blushing from shyness; nothing suggests he is ill.

B.why_wrong: The narrator says she and Mary “understood what his awkwardness meant” because they were shy too, so she sees him as shy, not rude.

D.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes how Mr. Gray behaves, not why he has come; the text never gives his reason for the visit.

sources.what: Gaskell, My Lady Ludlow (Gutenberg text): paragraph copied exactly; Mr. Gray is the new clergyman; the narrator and Mary Mason meet him in the great hall

items.notes: Literature (novella, 1858). Key C. Like 1.20 ('offers a detail that shows ...'), the underlined sentence gives details that show a feeling. A reads 'hotter-looking' literally, B reverses the narrator's attitude, D is invented.

items.passage: Chung Sai Yat Po was a Chinese-language newspaper published in San Francisco, California, from 1900 to 1951. Its founder, Ng Poon Chew, had originally established it as a weekly publication in Los Angeles in 1899 before relocating it to San Francisco and publishing it daily. The paper remained financially independent and unaffiliated with any political party, and Ng used it to advocate reforming certain traditional Chinese customs and to argue for equal rights for Chinese Americans, including women. It became one of the longest-running Chinese-language daily newspapers in the United States.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To provide an overview of a newspaper’s history and the causes it supported
To compare Chung Sai Yat Po with the English-language newspapers of San Francisco
To explain why Ng Poon Chew decided to move his newspaper from Los Angeles to San Francisco
To argue that Chinese-language newspapers should have supported political parties
items.explanation: The text gives the newspaper’s history, from its start “as a weekly publication in Los Angeles in 1899” to its run in San Francisco “from 1900 to 1951,” and describes what it stood for: Ng used it “to advocate reforming certain traditional Chinese customs and to argue for equal rights for Chinese Americans.” Choice A states this purpose.

B.why_wrong: The text never mentions English-language newspapers.

C.why_wrong: The text says the paper moved from Los Angeles to San Francisco but gives no reason for the move.

D.recipe: stance the text does not take (STANCE)
D.why_wrong: The text notes that the paper was “unaffiliated with any political party” but does not argue about what newspapers should have done.

sources.what: Chung Sai Yat Po (Wikipedia): founded by Ng Poon Chew; began as a weekly in Los Angeles in 1899, moved to San Francisco in 1900 and renamed; published 1900 to 1951; one of the longest running and most popular Chinese-language daily newspapers in the US; financially independent and non-party-affiliated; advocated reform of Chinese cultural practices and equal rights for Chinese Americans, including women

items.notes: Area: history (journalism). Key A. Like 1.6 ('an overview of the history and importance'), worded differently. The text does not call it the first Chinese daily, since the source does not. Distractors: B and C invented, D a stance.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Margaret Deland’s 1906 novel The Awakening of Helena Richie. Benjamin Wright, an elderly man, has invited his friend Dr. Lavendar into his dining room.

The room with its mammoth sideboard black with age and its solitary chair at one end of the long table, was lonely enough. On the walls, papered a generation ago with a drab paper sprinkled over with occasional pale gilt medallions, were some time-stained engravings: “The Destruction of Nineveh”; “The Trial of Effie Deans”; “The Death-bed of Washington.” A gloomy room at best; now, with the shutters of one window still bowed [closed], and the faint twitter of the canaries, and that one chair at the head of the table, it was very melancholy.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why the room’s owner keeps the shutters of his windows closed
To show that the room has recently been redecorated with new paper and engravings
To describe engravings that the room’s owner made when he was a young man
To emphasize the loneliness and gloom of a room
items.explanation: The text calls the room “lonely enough” and “a gloomy room at best,” and it ends by saying that “it was very melancholy.” Details such as the “solitary chair,” the “drab paper,” and the “time-stained engravings” support that impression. Choice D states this purpose.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions that one window’s shutters are “still bowed [closed]” but gives no reason for it.

B.why_wrong: The walls were “papered a generation ago” and the engravings are “time-stained,” so nothing has been recently redecorated.

C.why_wrong: The text lists the engravings’ titles but never says who made them.

sources.what: Deland, The Awakening of Helena Richie (New York: Harper, 1906; Gutenberg text): paragraph copied exactly except the opening 'And, indeed, the room' (adapted); gloss added; Benjamin Wright shows Dr. Lavendar into his dining room

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1906). Key D, short as easy keys often are (1.9 'establishes how the narrator feels about the piano'). Distractors: A partial, B reversal, C invented. Chosen over a fourth Jewett work to spread authors.

items.passage: Helen Cordero was a potter from Cochiti Pueblo in New Mexico who, in 1964, created her first Storyteller figure: a clay grandfather surrounded by five small children, inspired partly by her own grandfather, Santiago Quintana. items.passage: After the phonograph was invented in 1877, researchers began transporting the machines into the field to record songs and stories that communities had preserved through memory rather than writing. In 1890, anthropologist Jesse Walter Fewkes recorded Passamaquoddy songs, legends, and stories in Maine on 36 wax cylinders. Beginning in 1906, composer Percy Grainger used a phonograph to document folk singers in Lincolnshire, England, and composers Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály eventually recorded hundreds of cylinders of traditional melodies in Hungarian villages.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text describes a disagreement among composers, then explains how it was resolved.
The text explains how the phonograph worked, then compares it with later recording devices.
The text describes a new practice, then gives several examples of it.
The text presents a problem with early recordings, then describes efforts to restore them.
items.explanation: The first sentence describes a general development: researchers “began transporting the machines into the field to record songs and stories.” The next three sentences give examples: Fewkes in Maine, Grainger in Lincolnshire, and Bartók and Kodály in Hungary. Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text names several composers but describes no disagreement among them.

B.why_wrong: The text does not explain how the phonograph worked or mention later recording devices.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about damaged recordings or efforts to restore them.

sources.what: Library of Congress blog (Now See Hear!, 2023): Jesse Walter Fewkes borrowed a cylinder recording device from Thomas Edison in 1890 and traveled to Maine to record the Passamaquoddy community, recording 36 cylinders of songs, legends, stories and linguistic terms

items.passage: Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight and intensifies what is known as the urban heat island effect, in which cities become considerably hotter than the surrounding countryside. Hoping to reduce this heat on city streets, officials in Los Angeles, California, began in 2017 to coat selected streets with CoolSeal, a gray sealant that reflects more sunlight than conventional black asphalt does. The coating costs approximately $40,000 per mile and lasts for seven years, and early measurements indicated that the surface of coated pavement was about 10°F cooler than that of nearby uncoated pavement.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe a city’s effort to cool its streets and the early results
To argue that other cities should coat their streets with the same material
To compare the costs of several methods for lowering temperatures in cities
To explain why asphalt makes cities hotter than the surrounding countryside
items.explanation: The text explains that Los Angeles officials were “hoping to reduce this heat on city streets,” describes the coating they began applying in 2017, and reports that “the surface of coated pavement was about 10°F cooler” than that of uncoated pavement. Choice A states this purpose: an effort and its early results.

B.recipe: stance the text does not take (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: The text reports what Los Angeles did but never says other cities should do the same.

C.why_wrong: The text gives the cost of only one method, the coating.

D.why_wrong: Only the first sentence explains why asphalt makes cities hotter; the rest of the text is about the city’s response.

sources.what: Green Building Advisor, 'Los Angeles Lightens Streets in Bid to Stay Cool' (2017): heat island effect; CoolSeal, a gray-colored sealer that lowers road temperatures; city applying a reflective coating to some streets from May 2017; coated pavement surface 10 F cooler than an adjacent uncoated area; costs $40,000 a mile and lasts seven years

items.notes: Area: social science (urban policy). Key A, worded away from 1.8's 'an effort ... and some results of that effort'. Later research questioning the coating's effect on people's comfort is not part of this item.

items.passage: When a predator approaches, many animals flee, conceal themselves, or fight back. Others respond more unexpectedly: they stop moving and remain motionless, as if they were dead. <u>This behavior is known as thanatosis.</u> Although thanatosis may seem risky, it can improve an animal’s chances of survival. Biologist Takahisa Miyatake and colleagues investigated this possibility using red flour beetles, selectively breeding, over ten generations, one population that feigned death for long periods and another that did so only briefly. When a jumping spider was introduced, beetles from the long-feigning population were captured less frequently.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why some predators ignore prey that remains still.
It describes the result of an experiment involving red flour beetles.
It presents a hypothesis that the study discussed later fails to support.
It provides the name of a behavior that the rest of the text examines.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined one describes animals that “stop moving and remain motionless, as if they were dead.” The underlined sentence gives this behavior a name, “thanatosis,” and the rest of the text uses that term while describing a study of the behavior in beetles. Choice D states this function.

A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence only names the behavior; the text never explains why predators might ignore still prey.

B.recipe: the job of a later sentence (PART)
B.why_wrong: The experiment’s result is given in the last sentence, not in the underlined one.

C.why_wrong: The underlined sentence names a behavior rather than proposing a hypothesis, and the study described later supports the idea that the behavior can improve an animal’s chances of survival.

sources.what: Miyatake et al. (2004, Proceedings of the Royal Society B): death-feigning (thanatosis) in red flour beetles; two-way artificial selection for duration over 10 generations; predation by an Adanson jumping spider was lower among beetles from long-duration strains

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Key D, worded away from 1.11's key. The term is introduced without 1.11's 'Scientists call this process' frame. Distractors: A invented, B a later sentence's job, C a sibling label (REL).

notes: death-feigning also in live central_ideas_and_details w3b1_09 (moorland hawker dragonflies, Khelifa 2017): different animal, study and point
